papers.title: Fidelity-Aware Frequency Allocation and Transpilation Co-Design for Tunable Coupler Quantum Systems
papers.abstract: Frequency crowding is a fundamental limitation in superconducting quantum architectures, particularly in tunable-coupler systems. We present a framework that explicitly models both coherent spectator-induced errors and incoherent lifetime effects through an error budgeting approach. Using this model, we analyze how frequency crowding impacts gate fidelity as module size and connectivity scale, and formulate a constrained optimization problem to assign qubit and coupler frequencies under realistic separation and hardware constraints. We demonstrate scalable frequency allocation strategies that minimize spectator-induced errors. We further show that increasing qubit count and coupling density within a module leads to a fidelity-connectivity tradeoff. To explore the benefits at the system scale, we have developed a noise-aware transpilation approach called FINESSE, which minimizes error by selecting high-fidelity paths that satisfy connectivity via SWAP insertion while jointly optimizing downstream gate execution. We demonstrate this physics-informed architecture-transpilation co-design approach for a SNAIL-based third-order coupler that natively realizes the $\sqrt{iSWAP}$ basis with frequency aware gate fidelities. On SNAIL architectures, FINESSE achieves an average 8.9% reduction in log-infidelity cost and 6.8% reduction in circuit depth vs. SABRE. We also compare results on IBM Brisbane's architecture.

summary.summary: This paper presents a co-design framework connecting frequency allocation in SNAIL-based tunable-coupler systems to fidelity-aware circuit transpilation, introducing an error budgeting model that captures both spectator-induced coherent errors and $T_1$-limited incoherent losses. The work demonstrates that frequency crowding fundamentally limits module size to ~4 qubits while achieving >0.99 fidelity, and develops FINESSE, a noise-aware transpiler that achieves 8.9% reduction in log-infidelity cost over SABRE on SNAIL architectures.
summary.motivation: SNAIL-based tunable couplers enable flexible multi-qubit interactions but suffer from spectator-induced errors when qubits are tightly packed spectrally; balancing connectivity against fidelity degradation requires jointly optimizing hardware frequencies and circuit routing strategies.
summary.method: An error budgeting approach quantifies spectator-induced infidelity as $\propto 2x_0/(x_1+\delta)^2$ and incoherent loss as $\propto x_0/(x_1+\delta)$ as functions of frequency detuning $\delta$. A constrained optimization using Nelder-Mead assigns qubit and SNAIL frequencies under realistic bounds (3.3–5.7 GHz qubits, 4.2–4.7 GHz SNAIL, 200 MHz minimum spacing); FINESSE extends SABRE/MIRAGE transpilation by replacing hop-count distances with fidelity-weighted shortest paths using $L_{ij}=-\log\max(C_{ij}, 10^{-10})$ and joint mirror-gate acceptance criteria.
summary.result: Analysis shows gate fidelity is ~100× more sensitive to detuning for SNAIL-qubit conversion than qubit-qubit conversion; for $N=2,3,4,5$ qubits the geometric mean gate fidelities are 0.996, 0.994, 0.991, 0.940 respectively. On four-module SNAIL topologies, FINESSE achieves 8.9% log-infidelity reduction and 6.8% depth reduction versus SABRE; the 4-qubit 4-edge module provides optimal fidelity–connectivity tradeoff despite higher connectivity modules reducing routing overhead.

papers.title: Concatenating Algebraic Codes over High-Rate Quantum LDPC Codes
papers.abstract: Different quantum error correction schemes trade off overhead, error suppression, and hardware connectivity. Code concatenation can relax these tradeoffs by using an outer code whose non-local connectivity is supplied by logical operations of an inner code rather than directly by hardware. Prior works showed that this can reduce memory overhead for local low-rate inner codes such as the surface code. Here, we study concatenation over non-local, high-rate inner codes. Such inner codes experience correlated errors among the many logical qubits in a single codeblock. We handle this by treating each block as a single logical Galois qudit, enabling concatenation with algebraic outer codes with excellent parameters and, crucially, list decoders. In particular, we consider a memory system formed by concatenating quantum Reed-Solomon outer codes over the gross code. For fault-tolerant syndrome extraction, we develop a Galois qudit Shor scheme using "time-like" Reed-Solomon protection against measurement errors. Interestingly, a lightweight fault tolerance scheme, that would fail for qubits, works well for large-alphabet qudits, suggesting a very different theory of fault tolerance for such qudits. The whole protocol is optimised via improved bicycle instruction logical error rates, novel compilation strategies, and recent decoder post-selection rules. At uniform $10^{-3}$ physical noise, the concatenated gross code reaches the teraquop regime, which it previously could not access, with a lower space overhead than the $288$-qubit two-gross code, while offering several advantages from the engineering standpoint. Beyond our main case study, we believe the core ideas of Galois qudits, quantum Reed-Solomon outer codes, and list decoding, will prove generically powerful and highly transferable ideas across high-rate quantum architectures.

summary.summary: This paper concatenates quantum Reed–Solomon codes with large-alphabet Galois qudits ($q = 2048$) as outer codes over the 144-qubit gross bivariate bicycle code as inner code, reaching the teraquop regime (logical error rates $10^{-14}$–$10^{-13}$ per logical qubit-round) at uniform physical noise $p = 10^{-3}$ with lower space overhead than the 288-qubit two-gross code down to $4.1 \times 10^{-15}$ per logical qubit-round. The construction introduces spacetime error mixing to handle unknown logical error distributions of the inner code and demonstrates fault-tolerant syndrome extraction via Galois qudit Shor schemes with time-like Reed–Solomon codes protecting measurement errors.
summary.motivation: High-rate quantum LDPC codes like the gross code reduce space overhead compared to surface codes but require non-local connectivity; concatenation with outer codes relaxes this trade-off, enables modular architectures, and allows recovery from localized catastrophic errors.
summary.method: The 11 non-pivot logical qubits of each gross code are packaged into a single $q=2^{11}$-dimensional Galois qudit, enabling concatenation with quantum Reed–Solomon outer codes of parameters $[[n, n-2(d-1), d]]_q$. Fault-tolerant syndrome extraction uses qudit cat states prepared via repeated fault-tolerant measurements of weight-two stabilizers, with overcomplete syndrome bases protected by time-like Reed–Solomon codes. Spacetime error mixing averages over random qudit-to-qubit basis choices and linear combination parameters to bound failure probabilities using only aggregate inner-code statistics.
summary.result: At $p=10^{-3}$, the concatenated gross code achieves $\sim 4.1 \times 10^{-15}$ logical error rate per logical qubit-round with $<500\,000$ physical qubits and better space overhead than the 288-qubit two-gross code; list decoding of large-alphabet Reed–Solomon codes suppresses weight-3 and weight-4 error rates by factors $\sim n(d-M)/(q-1)^M$, a genuine advantage absent for qubits ($q=2$).
